chapter_theme: Akananuru 141 to 160, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems weigh wealth against parting from both sides (men who go, one who stays, women who consent, resolve to follow, or scorn the stay-at-home), two foster mothers mourn eloped girls, hill poems move secret meetings between day and night, and neythal and marutham poems press for marriage. Puram fame (Minjili and the fallen Eyinan, Kurukkai's punnai, Muziri's trade, Pittan, Nannan, Nalli, Aay) is used throughout as the measure of private feeling.

141.reading: Answering a friend who fears she cannot bear the parting, the woman says her dreams are sweet night after night, the house birds give good omens and her heart is eager: may he come back for the town's festival of lamps on the full-moon midnight of the six stars, he who crossed the Vengadam desert to bring wealth as famous as Karikal's town Idaiyaru.
141.nuance: Her answer to the friend's worry is a date, not resignation: she has fixed the Karthigai full moon as the night of his return. The wealth he went for is pictured not as gold but as a Chola town's household plenty (a new bride fed in her house, girls pounding fresh rice, a pregnant heron startled by the pestle), so even his errand is imagined as home.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits for a man who has crossed the desert for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the famous wealth he went to bring

142.reading: Leaving the night tryst, the man tells his heart to rejoice like the needy who carried full vessels away from Poraiyan Kadungo of Maantharam: she came at midnight, slowly, fearing that many would know, her dark hair swaying, walking like a doll that had learned to move, and embraced him till her bangle left its mark, speaking words sweet as tuned strings.
142.nuance: Lines 7 to 14 set a puram battle (Minjili killing Athikan, 'a protection to the birds', at Nannan's Paazhi) beside her coming, but how the battle attaches to the sentence is not clear in our text: it may measure his joy or her daring. The patron simile is pointed: he is a suppliant who has received.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்துநீங்குந் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a midnight meeting in secret love

comparisons.tenor: the red tongues of the noble praisers
the heart's fullness after her coming
the pollen dropping from her rain-soaked garland

143.reading: The friend tells the man that when he said, 'We will go, crossing the burning hills where the sun has stripped the teak and wind-fed fire roars in the clefts', at that small word the woman's eyes ran with tears like the blue lilies opened by spray in a pool on Kudhirai hill of Pittan, the Chera's warrior who showers fine vessels on those who live by hope; and the friend grieves.
143.nuance: The long, vivid account of the road is the man's own speech, quoted back; the friend's reply is one phrase, 'small word', and the tears. The colophon says it worked: he gave up the journey.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரியக்கருதிய தலைகனைத் தோழி தலைமகளது ஆற்றாமை கண்டுசெலவழுங்குவித்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: a man proposes to leave for work across the desert

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon does not say whether this is before or after marriage

144.reading: His war done, the man tells his heart (for the charioteer to hear) that his wife may say the days he promised have proved false, her tears will not stop, he forgets her hair bare of mullai garlands, he has no fear of wrong; but on the day his people hurry home to tell of the wealth won in battle, from a camp where the rutting elephant trumpets back at the thunder, she will rejoice as if she already had the embrace that ends all sulking.
144.nuance: He imagines her complaint in her own words before he imagines her joy, and her joy comes from the news before he arrives: the report of the victory does the work of the embrace (துனிதீர் முயக்கம் பெற்றோள் போல).

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting through the rains for a man at war

comparisons.tenor: her joy at the news of victory
the blood glittering here and there on the field

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்), spoken to as if to his own heart

145.reading: The foster mother hears that her girl has crossed with her man the empty, sun-stripped forest where cicadas shrill like chariot bells and a tiger-wounded elephant roars like thunder; and she curses her own hand, which in the rich father's house once seized the girl's small hair and beat her till the stick broke: may it come to harsh ruin like the punnai felled at Kurukkai in the war of Anni and Thithiyan.
145.nuance: The curse falls on her own hand, not on the man who took the girl: the elopement is read back as the result of her harshness at home. The girl who tired after a single step in her father's house is set against the road she has now crossed.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl has left with her lover across the desert

comparisons.tenor: the hand that beat the girl, cursed to ruin

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: she grieves aloud; no hearer is named

146.reading: Refusing the bard sent to plead for her husband, the woman says that if his tall belled chariot will not stop going for days on end to the street of the bright-jewelled women, then whoever she is, the woman who now trusts that deceiving philanderer's word as she once did will weep like a wind-shaken flower dripping dew, go pale, and give up the beauty her mother guarded.
146.nuance: She speaks of the new woman with pity rather than anger (அளியள்), and the pity is self-description: எம்போல், like me. The opening buffalo, which spends the day in the flowered pond and then lies down by a young cow near the garden, carries the charge without her stating it.

colophon.thurai: வாயில் வேண்டிச் சென்றபாணற்குத் தலைமகள் வாயில் மறுத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife refuses her husband's go-between over his other women

comparisons.tenor: the new woman's tears dropping on her breast
the new woman who trusts him as the speaker once did

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the new young woman he has taken up

pairs.situation: he spends his days roaming the courtesans' quarter
he takes up a young new woman
he settles near the home but not in it

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the buffalo of her own town's fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

147.reading: Told by her friend that the man is leaving, the woman says that, like Velli Veethi, she has made herself ready to go on that endless forked road where a spotted tiger listens for the stag's call to feed his mate, starving in a rock cleft after bearing three cubs; wasting unfed, her shoulders losing their beauty, grieving daily for his return, she has no will to stay behind, since there is no other medicine.
147.nuance: Velli Veethi is the name of a woman poet (Akananuru 45 is under her name); the heroine claims her as a precedent for a woman who goes after the man. The hungry tigress fed by her mate, and the woman who does not eat (உண்ணா உயக்கம்), stand a few lines apart.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman about to be left resolves to follow on the desert road

comparisons.tenor: her own resolve to go after the man

iraicchi.act: the male tiger hunts for his mate, who is starving in her cleft after giving birth
iraicchi.sense: on the very road he will take, the beast provides for its mate in her need, while he leaves her to waste unfed

148.reading: To the man of the land where a rutting elephant, after smashing trees and goring a tiger, raids the millet field, the friend says the girl's distress is great, like the owl that, ashamed when Aay Eyinan fell fighting Minjili, does not go abroad in broad day; so he must come at nightfall, by the small stony path where the great tusker grazes shoots.
148.nuance: The owl's shame belongs to the Eyinan legend in which the birds shaded the fallen hero from the sun: the night bird could not join them. The friend turns that daylight shame into the reason the meetings must move from day to night. The raiding elephant of the address may hint at his daytime visits to the field she guards, but the poem never makes the match.

thinai_evidence.note: hill slopes, millet fields and elephants

comparisons.tenor: the girl's distress at day meetings

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon does not name the speaker; the friend speaks of the girl as இவள்

149.reading: The man tells his heart he will not go down the long desert road, where bears raid the iruppai blossoms when tired of termites, even if the precious wealth that is hard to win came easily, for it would fill with tears her eyes, which are like the paired blue lilies of the deep pool on the Tall One's hill west of Koodal, the city of Chezhiyan, who stormed Muziri where Yavana ships come with gold and leave with pepper.
149.nuance: He refuses not hard-won wealth but wealth gained easily, the strongest form of the refusal. Muziri's trade, gold in and pepper out, stands in the same sentence, so the richest wealth the poet knows is weighed against one woman's tears.

thinai_evidence.note: a man gives up the journey for wealth across the desert

150.reading: The friend tells the man who comes for day meetings that the mother, seeing the girl's hair now loosed from its braid, the gold spots budding on her chest and her breasts rising, praised her, held her close, thought long, and put her under strict guard; and since he left, every time the girl sees the backwater and the shore grove where neythal closes at evening and opens with the kaavi at morning, she grieves, asking whether he will not come.
150.nuance: The mother's praise and embrace are themselves the act of confinement: the signs of the girl's coming of age are what close the house to her. The flowers that close at dusk and open at dawn mark the days she counts.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்துகண்ணுற்று நீங்கும் தலைமகனைத் தோழி தலைமகளை இடத்துய்த்து வந்து, செறிப்பறிவுறீஇ வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, shore grove and neythal flowers

comparisons.tenor: the pallor spots on her chest

151.reading: The woman tells her friend that the man, holding that the poor cannot support those who depend on them nor laugh at ease among their kin, has a heart set on great wealth for which grace counts for nothing, and has crossed the forest where uzhinjil pods rattle like a dancer's drum in the wind, and a small red-tongued lizard by a cairn's withered shade tells travellers what will befall them.
151.nuance: She quotes his reason fairly before judging it: the maxim is about duty to dependants and kin, not greed, and her complaint is only that it leaves no room for grace (அருள் பிறிது). The cairn and the omen-lizard put death and chance on the road his reason sends him down.

thinai_evidence.note: a man has crossed the forest in search of wealth

comparisons.tenor: the forked branches of the uzhinjil
the rattling of the dry pods

152.reading: Leaving the night tryst, the man tells his heart that the woman who came to end his trembling grief and is now going home to her small hill village, her curled hair like the peacock's train on the Ezhil hill at Nannan's Paazhi, her shoulders fragrant beyond the kaandhal of Nalli's slopes and smooth as the bamboo on the crags of Aay's forest, still gives him trembling pain though she is far away.
152.nuance: The chain of patrons (Thithan Veliyan's shore, Pindan defeated by Nannan, Nalli, Aay) is used only to grade her beauty: every great man's land supplies one feature. The phrase about Aay, who gives to all who come 'whether able or not', is a patron's praise carried whole into a love poem.

thinai_evidence.note: hill village, kaandhal and bamboo

153.reading: The foster mother grieves that the girl, who used to tire even chasing a ball with her sweet-voiced friends, has now trusted a hard man's chest and sweet words and gone without a thought for their sorrow into the summer forest where wind-struck bamboo throws up sparks and fire; she asks whether those soft feet can bear the barren desert under the dark hill, where at night kongu flowers fall like lamps let slip from the hand against a starry sky.
153.nuance: The only beauty in the poem is at the end, and it is a night image of falling lights on the hill the girl must pass under: the mother's fear and her eye for the land are in the same line.

thinai_evidence.note: the scorched summer forest and the barren way

comparisons.tenor: the hill crest strewn with lit kongu flowers at night

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: she grieves aloud; no hearer is named

154.reading: His work done, the man bids the charioteer drive fast over the rain-washed woodland, where frogs croak like many small instruments, pidavu blossoms streak the red sand, kodal buds open like a cobra's raised hood, and the twist-horned stag drinks clear water and rests in safety with his mate, so they may hasten to the lovely woman whose ways are bent on him.
154.nuance: The stag drinks and rests 'in safety' (ஏமுற) with his mate: the word for the beasts' ease is the word another homecoming poem uses for the man's own heart (Akananuru 34).

thinai_evidence.note: rain-washed woodland on the road home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன், வலவ)

iraicchi.act: the stag drinks clear water and rests in safety beside his mate
iraicchi.sense: the man, his work done, means to come home and rest with his wife as the stag does with his mate

155.reading: The woman tells her friend that the man who stroked her hair saying 'A life that never comes to the door of wrong, and wealth that never goes to another's door: both come from wealth, my jewelled one' may finish his work though she suffers; he has crossed the hills where the marul withers, where in Paan country the tiger's pugmarks in an elephant's footprint by a herdsmen's dried well look like finger marks pressed into a drum's head.
155.nuance: She consents in his own words, and the consent is real (தாந்தம் செய்வினை முடிக்க), but the two goods his maxim names are virtue and independence; the pleasure of the household, which his going costs, is not among them.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman endures a man's absence on his errand for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the tiger's pugmarks in the elephant's footprint

156.reading: The friend tells the lord of the town, where guards fence the drooping rice ears from an old cow with gourd vines and cotton, that since she and the girl, playing in the fields in leaf skirts of ambal, met him, the girl's gem-dark skin has turned gold with pallor, and her mother, weeping and finding no cure, offers toddy, garlands and a white goat to the god of the ford: was it their fault?
156.nuance: The mother treats the pallor as a god's seizure and sacrifices for it; the friend lets the man know that only he can cure it. Line 12 (நின்நகாப் பிழைத்த தவறே) is hard and we cannot fix whose laughing or not laughing is the fault. The guarded rice may point to the girl's guarded youth, but the poem does not name the guarding, so it is left as scene.

colophon.thurai: தலை மகளைஇடத்துய்த்துவந்த தோழி தலைமகனை வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: rice fields, ford and the town lord; the human situation is courtship, not quarrel

157.reading: The woman tells her friend that men who mean to go alone down the fearful road, where red-eyed bowmen drunk on palm toddy roar for war and a forest elephant at dawn eats the athiral creeper that bloomed by night over the cairns of the slain, would speak such heart-consuming words only to women able to stay home, withering like a ruined painted doll in the deserted square of a raided village.
157.nuance: She defines the woman who can be left as a thing already ruined, a doll rotted by rain and sun in an emptied village; by implication she is not that woman, and his words are wasted on her.

thinai_evidence.note: the bandit road with cairns of the slain

comparisons.tenor: the woman who can stay behind, withering

158.reading: With the man listening nearby, the friend tells the foster mother not to torment the girl for what she says she saw at midnight after the storm, earrings flashing like lightning, swaying like a peacock coming down a hill: on their garden hill spirits come in any form they please and dreams fool sleepers like waking truth, and this girl shivers alone without a lamp, runs for shelter when the owl hoots in the kadamba, and with their fierce father away would she ever dare such a thing?
158.nuance: The defence offers two explanations (a hill spirit, a dream) and a character witness (her timidity), and every word of it also reaches the hidden lover: the mother has seen, and the night meetings cannot go on.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன்சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி செவிலித்தாய்க்குச்சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: midnight after rain on the hill

comparisons.tenor: the father's pack of hunting dogs

159.reading: The friend tells the woman not to grieve that her lover has crossed the forked road where bowmen, back from raiding cattle on the frontier, cook meat to the beat of the tudi beside the cold hearth stones left by salt carters; even if he reached Aamur with its high walls east of Vaanavan's hill, where that king broke the tusks of elephants, he is not a man to stay there and forget her breast.
159.nuance: The road's dangers are named only to be set aside: the comfort rests not on the road being safe but on the man's attachment outlasting even a famous city.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend comforts a woman whose man has crossed the desert

160.reading: The friend asks the girl whether her heart too is trembling: the chariot of the lord of the shore, where the open-mouthed male turtle guards the eggs his mate buried in the white sand until they hatch, used to come at night, the driver easing the horse through the backwater so the wheel cut the neythal buds, which rose like snakes' raised heads; now it has come by day, openly, with shouting young men, for the noisy little village to see.
160.nuance: Night against day, hiding against showing (கரவாது): the chariot's daylight arrival is the public sign of marriage, and the village whose gossip was the danger is now the witness.

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, turtle and neythal on the shore

iraicchi.act: the male turtle guards the eggs his mate buried in the sand until they hatch
iraicchi.sense: the man who now comes openly will guard her and their household as the turtle guards its brood

links.note: Both are Paranar's and both tell of Aay Eyinan falling to Minjili: in 208 the birds gather to shade the fallen man from the sun; in 148 the owl, ashamed, does not go out by day to see him.
links.teaches: Read together they show the legend had a second bird in it: the night owl that could not join the daylight shading, and the poet uses that one bird's shame as a reason for lovers to meet by night.

links.note: In 142 the man Minjili killed at Nannan's Paazhi is Athikan, 'a protection to the birds' (புள்ளிற்கு ஏமம்); in 181 it is Aay Eyinan who falls to Minjili and a flock of birds hides the sun over him.
links.teaches: The epithet in 142 is explained by the scene in 181, but the name differs, so the bird-shade legend either belonged to one hero known by two names or moved between heroes of the Paazhi wars.

links.note: Both use the felling of the old punnai at Kurukkai in the war of Anni and Thithiyan: in 45 the gossip is louder than the bards' cheers that day; in 145 the foster mother curses her own hand to be cut down like that tree.
links.teaches: One puram event served the akam poets as a measure of two different things, public noise in one poem and deserved ruin in the other, so the war's fame had become a store of ready comparisons.

links.note: Purananuru 170 praises Pittan as soft to those who come in hope (நசைவர்க்கு மென்மை) and iron to enemies; Akananuru 143 calls him the giver of fine vessels to those who live by hope (நசையின் வாழ்நர்க்கு) and sets the woman's tears in a pool on his hill.
links.teaches: The akam poet takes from Pittan's fame the same formula of giving to the hopeful that the praise poem uses, which shows a patron's epithet passing whole between the two kinds of poetry.

links.note: In Purananuru 343 a father refuses suitors even if they bow and offer wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) like Muziri's, where ships bring gold for pepper; in Akananuru 149 the man refuses precious wealth (விழுப்பொருள்) even if easily won, beside Muziri where Yavana ships bring gold and take pepper.
links.teaches: Muziri's sea trade was the stock measure of the wealth a woman outweighs, used by the war poem for a father keeping his daughter and by the love poem for a husband keeping his wife.

links.note: Akananuru 152 names Aay as the one who gives to all who come, whether able or not (வல்லினும் வல்லார் ஆயினும்); Purananuru 134 says Aay is no trader in virtue who gives in this life for a return in the next.
links.teaches: Together they make Aay's giving unconditional on both sides, asking nothing of the receiver's skill and nothing of the next world, which neither poem says alone.

links.note: The man's maxim quoted in 151 is that the poor cannot support their dependants or laugh among their kin; Kural 1047 says poverty makes a man a stranger even to the mother who bore him.
links.teaches: The Kural states as a rule the claim the akam hero uses to justify leaving, and the poem shows what the rule costs when it is acted on: the wife says it leaves no room for grace.

links.note: Kural 760 says that for those who make bright wealth the other two (virtue and pleasure) come easily together; in Akananuru 155 the man says two things come from wealth, a life free of wrong and a wealth that never begs, and leaves.
links.teaches: The hero's version of the Kural's claim drops pleasure from the pair, and the poem makes that omission visible: the household pleasure is exactly what his errand for wealth suspends.

links.note: Both answer the man's announced departure: in Kural 1151 the reply (the friend's or the woman's) is a sharp refusal, tell your quick return to those who will survive; in Akananuru 143 the friend only reports the woman's tears at his 'small word', and the colophon says he stayed.
links.teaches: The same thurai had two answers, the Kural's barbed argument and the Sangam friend's report of tears, and the poem shows the second one succeeding, which the couplet's general statement cannot show.

links.note: In 149 the man says even easily won wealth is not worth her tears and stays; in 155 the man holds that virtue and independence both come only from wealth, and goes. On the plain reading they are incompatible verdicts on whether wealth justifies the parting.
links.teaches: The anthology sets the paalai argument on both sides in the men's own voices, so the case for going and the case for staying are each given their strongest form.

links.note: Both are a foster mother's lament after the girl has eloped across the desert; 153 blames the girl's trust in a hard man and fears for her soft feet, 145 turns the blame on the speaker's own hand that once beat her.
links.teaches: Together they give the two directions of the mother's grief in this thurai, outward to the girl's heedlessness and inward to her own harshness, both ending on the girl's tender body set against the road.

links.note: Both are the homecoming man's words to his charioteer, and both put a stag with twisted horns (திரிமருப்பு இரலை, இருதிரி மருப்பின் இரலை) by clear water (தெள்அறல்) caring for or resting with his mate, with the word ஏமுற.
links.teaches: Shared phrases across two poets show the stag with his mate is a fixed formula of this thurai, and in 34 ஏமுற is the man's own heart's ease while in 154 it is the beasts', so the formula passes the same rest from beast to man.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage: the formal union that ends secret love, sought or pressed for in the akam poems
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons' word (வரைவு கடாயது, வரைவு மலிந்து)

source_issues: 143: the colophon thurai reads தலைகனைத், a misprint for தலைமகனைத்.
146: line 6 reads ஒள்ளிமழை, apparently a misprint for ஒள்ளிழை (bright-jewelled); line 8 reads அனியள், apparently for அளியள் (pitiable). Marked as the poem plainly means.
147: the base text has 14 lines and the commentary edition (pmuni0523_01) 13; marked as the base text stands.
155: line 15 reads வடுவில், where a comparison (வடுவின்) seems meant; recorded as a comparison without a marker.
157: the base text numbers the last line 15 though the poem has 14 lines; a misprinted number.
